title: Data the endpoint should not return
brief: 17:40. The profile screen shows a name and a photo. A researcher opened the network tab and found a lot more in the response.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: The app only displays the name. The server sends the whole row.
teaches: The server decides what a response contains, not the client
Return an explicit list of fields for each audience
Password hashes and internal flags never belong in an API response

value.title: User API

lines: res.json(user);                 // the whole row, the app picks what to show
// columns: id, displayName, photoUrl, email, phone, pwHash,

value.intro: Open the profile screen, then look at what actually arrives over the wire.

attempts.label: Read the raw JSON response
attempts.response:
HTTP 200
{ "id": 88, "displayName": "Megan Holt", "photoUrl": "...",
  "email": "megan@customer.test", "phone": "07700 900311",
  "pwHash": "5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99",
  "internalNotes": "chargeback dispute Oct, watch",

The password hash, the fraud score and a staff note, for anyone who can call the API.

attempts.label: Read another user's profile the same way
attempts.response:
HTTP 200
{ ...another customer's email, phone, hash and notes... }

fix.prompt: Pick every change that makes the server decide exactly what leaves, and takes things that should never leave out of reach.

options.label: Return an explicit response shape with only the fields each audience needs
code: + res.json({ id: user.id, displayName: user.displayName, photoUrl: user.photoUrl });
options.why: A new column added tomorrow does not leak by default. The response lists what is allowed.

options.label: Give staff and internal fields their own role gated endpoint
options.why: Support can still see what they need, and nobody else can.

options.label: Never load the password hash and fraud score into API code at all
options.why: Data that never reaches the handler cannot be returned by a mistake.

options.label: Hide the extra fields in the app's code
code: + const { displayName, photoUrl } = response;   // ignore the rest
options.why: The data still travels over the network. Anyone with a proxy or the network tab reads all of it.

options.label: Compress the response
options.why: Compression hides nothing from the person receiving the response.

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first
outcome.what: Reading the code before attacking it tells you where to look, and why it fails.
outcome.ideal: reads the code under review before trying to break it.

outcome.label: Tried normal use first
outcome.what: Knowing what a good request looks like is how you spot a bad one.
outcome.ideal: establishes normal behaviour before testing the abnormal.

outcome.label: Checked normal use still works
outcome.what: A fix that breaks real users gets reverted, and the bug comes back.
outcome.ideal: tests that the fix did not break normal use.

exploit.objective: Reproduce the bug: read the Code tab, then use the Exploit tab on staging.
exploit.insight: The app only displays the name. The server sends the whole row.

hint.text: Open the Workbench. Read the code, try normal use on the Exploit tab, then send the request that breaks it.

outcome.label: Reproduced the bug
outcome.what: The screen only displayed a name and a photo, but the API returned the whole database row: a password hash, a fraud score, a staff note. Anyone who can call the endpoint, or open the network tab, reads them all.
outcome.ideal: proves a bug is real before fixing it.

card.title: The app showed a name. The wire carried the rest
body: The screen only displayed a name and a photo, but the API returned the whole database row: a password hash, a fraud score, a staff note. Anyone who can call the endpoint, or open the network tab, reads them all.
And with no ownership check, they can read other people's too.
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: An explicit response shape means only named fields are returned, and a new sensitive column cannot leak by accident. Internal fields live behind a staff only route, and the hash never even reaches the handler.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: The server lists what leaves
body: An explicit response shape means only named fields are returned, and a new sensitive column cannot leak by accident. Internal fields live behind a staff only route, and the hash never even reaches the handler.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: Ignoring fields in the app changes what the screen draws. The response still contains everything, and it takes one proxy or the browser's network tab to read it.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: Hidden on screen, wide open on the wire
body: Ignoring fields in the app changes what the screen draws. The response still contains everything, and it takes one proxy or the browser's network tab to read it.
The server decides what is returned.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
